cmimc-2024-geometry-01.title: Coordinates
cmimc-2024-geometry-01.body:
Put $A=(0,0)$, $B=(5,0)$, $C=(5,h)$, $D=(0,h)$, so $E=(4,0)$ and $F=(1,h)$. Then $P=(2,2\sqrt3)$ (apex of the equilateral triangle on $AE$) and $Q=(3,h-2\sqrt3)$ (apex on $CF$, pointing down).

The line $EP$ has direction $(-2,2\sqrt3)$, i.e. slope $-\sqrt3$; it passes through $E=(4,0)$ and reaches $x=1$ at $y=3\sqrt3$. Since $F=(1,h)$ lies on it, $h=3\sqrt3$. Check: at $x=3$ the line has $y=\sqrt3=h-2\sqrt3$, so $Q$ is on it too.

**Answer: $3\sqrt3$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-01.title: Horizontal distances
cmimc-2024-geometry-01.body:
$AE=4$ means $EB=1$, and $P$ is $2$ to the right of $A$ (directly above the midpoint of $AE$), $E$ is $2$ to the right of $P$'s projection. The horizontal gap between $P$ and $Q$ equals $EB=1$, while $F$ and $Q$ are horizontally $2$ apart, so $E$ and $F$ are $3$ apart horizontally. Along the line $EF$ (slope at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal, the direction of side $EP$) the rise is $3\tan60^\circ=3\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $3\sqrt3$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-02.title: Two circular segments
cmimc-2024-geometry-02.body:
The circle $\Gamma_1$ centered at $A$ through $C$ has radius $AC=\sqrt3$ and also passes through $E$ (since $AE=AC$). The circle $\Gamma_2$ centered at $D$ through $E$ has radius $DE=1$ and also passes through $C$. So the circles meet at $C$ and $E$, and $CE=\sqrt3$, so $\triangle ACE$ is equilateral.

The centers $A$ and $D$ lie on opposite sides of chord $CE$, so the intersection is the union of two circular segments cut off by $CE$:

- in $\Gamma_1$: central angle $\angle CAE=60^\circ$, sector area $\frac16\pi\cdot3=\frac\pi2$, minus $[ACE]=\frac{\sqrt3}4\cdot3=\frac{3\sqrt3}4$;
- in $\Gamma_2$: central angle $\angle CDE=120^\circ$, sector area $\frac13\pi$, minus $[CDE]=\frac12\sin120^\circ=\frac{\sqrt3}4$.

Total: $\frac\pi2+\frac\pi3-\frac{3\sqrt3}4-\frac{\sqrt3}4=\frac{5\pi}6-\sqrt3$.

**Answer: $\frac{5\pi}{6}-\sqrt3$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-02.title: Numerical check
cmimc-2024-geometry-02.body:
Placing the hexagon with circumradius $1$ and counting grid points inside both circles gives an area of about $0.8859$, matching $\frac{5\pi}6-\sqrt3\approx0.88594$.

**Answer: $\frac{5\pi}{6}-\sqrt3$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-03.title: Coordinates
cmimc-2024-geometry-03.body:
Let $W=(0,0)$, $X=(w,0)$, $Z=(0,2)$ (the rectangle has height $2$ since $C_1$ touches both $WX$ and $YZ$). Then $O_1=(1,1)$, $O_2=(w-\frac12,\frac12)$, and $O_3$ has $y$-coordinate $2-\frac23=\frac43$.

$O_1O_3=1+\frac23=\frac53$ with vertical difference $\frac43-1=\frac13$, so the horizontal difference is $\sqrt{\frac{25}9-\frac19}=\frac{2\sqrt6}3$ and $O_3=(1+\frac{2\sqrt6}3,\frac43)$.

$O_2O_3=\frac12+\frac23=\frac76$ with vertical difference $\frac43-\frac12=\frac56$, so the horizontal difference is $\sqrt{\frac{49}{36}-\frac{25}{36}}=\frac{\sqrt6}3$, hence $O_2=(1+\sqrt6,\frac12)$.

Shoelace with $O_1=(1,1)$, $O_2=(1+\sqrt6,\frac12)$, $O_3=(1+\frac{2\sqrt6}3,\frac43)$: area $=\frac12\left|\sqrt6\cdot\frac13-\frac{2\sqrt6}3\cdot(-\frac12)\right|=\frac12\left(\frac{\sqrt6}3+\frac{\sqrt6}3\right)=\frac{\sqrt6}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt6}{3}$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-03.title: Bounding rectangle
cmimc-2024-geometry-03.body:
The bounding box of the three centers has width $\sqrt6$ and height $\frac56$ (area $\frac{5\sqrt6}6$). Subtract the three right triangles in the corners: $\frac{\sqrt6}9$, $\frac{5\sqrt6}{36}$ and $\frac{\sqrt6}4$. The remaining area is $\frac{(30-4-5-9)\sqrt6}{36}=\frac{\sqrt6}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{\sqrt6}{3}$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-04.title: Subtract two small triangles
cmimc-2024-geometry-04.body:
Since $\angle EBD=\angle FCG=45^\circ$, the lines $BE$ and $CG$ meet at $X$ with $\angle BXC=90^\circ$, so $BXC$ is an isosceles right triangle with hypotenuse $BC=1$ and area $\frac14$. The intersection of the two triangles is $\triangle BXC$ minus the two small corner pieces near $B$ and $C$ that lie outside $\triangle BDE$/$\triangle CFG$, which together have area $BF^2$ (twice the area of $\triangle BFY$ where $Y=FG\cap BE$).

In $\triangle CFG$ the right angle is at $F$, so $GF=FC$; in $\triangle BFG$ (right angle at $F$, $\angle B=60^\circ$) $GF=\sqrt3\,BF$. With $BF+FC=1$ this gives $BF=\frac{\sqrt3-1}2$. Then $BF^2=\frac{4-2\sqrt3}4$ and the area is $\frac14-\frac{4-2\sqrt3}4=\frac{2\sqrt3-3}4$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt3-3}{4}$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-04.title: Coordinates
cmimc-2024-geometry-04.body:
Take $B=(0,0)$, $C=(1,0)$. Right isosceles $BDE$ with right angle at $D$: $E=(d,d)$ on $AC$ ($y=-\sqrt3(x-1)$) gives $d=\frac{\sqrt3}{1+\sqrt3}$. By symmetry $\triangle CFG$ has $F=(1-d,0)$, $G=(1-d,d)$. A fine grid count of the overlap gives $0.1161$, matching $\frac{2\sqrt3-3}4\approx0.1160$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt3-3}{4}$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-05.title: Angle bisector
cmimc-2024-geometry-05.body:
Right triangles $APD$ and $APE$ share the hypotenuse $AP$ and have $AD=AE$, so they are congruent (HL). Hence $AP$ bisects $\angle A$ and $PD=PE$. The area of $ABC$ is $84$ (Heron), and also $\frac12(AB+AC)\cdot PD=14PD$, so $PD=PE=6$.

By the angle bisector theorem $PC=14\cdot\frac{15}{28}=\frac{15}2$. In right triangle $CEP$: $EC=\sqrt{(15/2)^2-6^2}=\frac92$. So $AE=AC-EC=15-\frac92=\frac{21}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{21}2$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-05.title: Numerical check
cmimc-2024-geometry-05.body:
Placing $B=(0,0)$, $C=(14,0)$, $A=(5,12)$ and scanning $P$ along $BC$ for $AD=AE$ gives $AD=10.5$.

**Answer: $\frac{21}2$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-06.title: The extreme slice
cmimc-2024-geometry-06.body:
Let the base have side length $1$ and let the base vertices be $A,B,\dots,H$ (top vertices $A',\dots,H'$). Cutting the prism in half means the plane passes through its center. Take the plane through $A$, $C$, the midpoint $X$ of edge $DD'$, then $E'$, $G'$ and the midpoint $Y$ of $HH'$: this cross-section is a hexagon with two sides $AC$ and $E'G'$ of length $\sqrt{2+\sqrt2}$ (diagonal of the regular octagon skipping one vertex) and four slanted sides $CX$, $XE'$, $G'Y$, $YA$.

Each slanted side has length $\sqrt{1+(h/2)^2}$ (horizontal run $CD=1$, vertical rise $h/2$). Equilateral means $1+\frac{h^2}4=2+\sqrt2$, so $h^2=4(1+\sqrt2)$ and $h=2\sqrt{1+\sqrt2}\approx3.11$.

Other hexagonal slices use a longer base chord (e.g. from $A$ to a point of $CD$ other than $C$), which forces longer slanted sides and hence a larger height, so this slice gives the minimum.

**Answer: $2\sqrt{1+\sqrt2}$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-06.title: Numerical search
cmimc-2024-geometry-06.body:
Searching numerically over all planes through the center of the prism (normal directions) and over heights $h$ for a hexagonal cross-section with equal sides finds no solution for $h<3.1$ and solutions from $h\approx3.107=2\sqrt{1+\sqrt2}$ upward.

**Answer: $2\sqrt{1+\sqrt2}$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-07.title: Three regular tetrahedra
cmimc-2024-geometry-07.body:
A vertex $A$ with exactly three neighbors $B_1,B_2,B_3$ has three faces around it, so $AB_1B_2B_3$ is a regular tetrahedron of edge $2$. The same holds for the other degree-3 vertex $A'$ with neighbors $B_1',B_2',B_3'$. Euler's formula gives $6$ vertices in total ($E=12$, $V=2-F+E=6$), so the two tetrahedra share two vertices: $B_1=B_1'$ and $B_2=B_2'$ (these two get five neighbors). The remaining $B_3,B_3'$ are joined by an edge of length $2$, which makes degree $4$ for each and the faces $B_1B_3B_3'$, $B_2B_3B_3'$ equilateral. This is the 'boat' (tritetrahedron).

It decomposes into three regular tetrahedra of edge $2$: $AB_1B_2B_3$, $A'B_1B_2B_3'$ and $B_1B_2B_3B_3'$. Each has volume $\frac{2^3\sqrt2}{12}=\frac{2\sqrt2}3$, so the volume is $3\cdot\frac{2\sqrt2}3=2\sqrt2$.

**Answer: $2\sqrt2$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-08.title: Mixtilinear incircles
cmimc-2024-geometry-08.body:
Triangle $ABC$ is right-angled, so its hypotenuse is a diameter of $\Omega$ and the sides are $\frac65R,\frac85R,2R$. The two tangent lines share one of the points, say $A$, so they are the lines $AB$ and $AC$, and $\omega$ is the $A$-mixtilinear incircle of $ABC$, of radius $r\sec^2\frac A2$ where $r=\frac{2}{5}R$ is the inradius.

The three choices of the shared vertex $A$ give: $A$ between sides $\frac85R,2R$ with $\cos A=\frac45$, $\sec^2\frac A2=\frac{10}9$, so $1=\frac25R\cdot\frac{10}9$, $R=\frac94$; $A$ the right angle ($\sec^2 45^\circ=2$): $1=\frac25R\cdot2$, $R=\frac54$; $A$ between $\frac65R,2R$ with $\cos A=\frac35$, $\sec^2\frac A2=\frac54$: $1=\frac25R\cdot\frac54$, $R=2$.

Sum: $\frac94+\frac54+2=\frac{11}2$.

**Answer: $\frac{11}{2}$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-09.title: The eight-point circle
cmimc-2024-geometry-09.body:
The midpoints of the sides form a parallelogram (Varignon), and being cyclic it is a rectangle, so $AC\perp BD$. Then $a^2+c^2=b^2+d^2$ for the sides in order, so opposite sides are $\{1,3\}$ and $\{\sqrt2,2\sqrt2\}$.

For a quadrilateral with perpendicular diagonals, the four midpoints and the feet of the perpendiculars from each midpoint to the opposite side (maltitude feet) lie on one circle (the eight-point circle), because the midpoints form a rectangle and each foot sees a diameter at a right angle. So $M,N,P$ lie on the circle through the four midpoints, which is the circumcircle of $MNP$. Its diameter is the diagonal of the rectangle, $\frac12\sqrt{AC^2+BD^2}$, so its area is $\pi\frac{AC^2+BD^2}{16}$.

For a cyclic quadrilateral, $AC^2=\frac{(ac+bd)(ad+bc)}{ab+cd}$ and $BD^2=\frac{(ac+bd)(ab+cd)}{ad+bc}$. Here $ac+bd=1\cdot3+\sqrt2\cdot2\sqrt2=7$, and $\{ab+cd,ad+bc\}=\{5\sqrt2,7\sqrt2\}$ in some order, so $AC^2+BD^2=7\left(\frac{7\sqrt2}{5\sqrt2}+\frac{5\sqrt2}{7\sqrt2}\right)=7\cdot\frac{74}{35}=\frac{74}5$. The area is $\frac{74}{5}\cdot\frac\pi{16}=\frac{37\pi}{40}$ for every valid arrangement (so 'greatest possible' is moot).

**Answer: $\frac{37\pi}{40}$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-09.title: Numerical check
cmimc-2024-geometry-09.body:
Enumerating all orderings of the four sides, the perpendicular-diagonal condition holds exactly when opposite sides are $(1,3)$ and $(\sqrt2,2\sqrt2)$, and each such ordering gives $\frac{\pi(AC^2+BD^2)}{16}=2.90597\ldots=\frac{37\pi}{40}$.

**Answer: $\frac{37\pi}{40}$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-10.title: Orthocenter and nine-point circle
cmimc-2024-geometry-10.body:
Let $AC$ and $BD$ meet at $P$. Since $\angle ACB=\angle ADB=90^\circ$, $E=AD\cap BC$ is the orthocenter of $\triangle PAB$, and $PE\perp AB$. The circumcenter of the circle through $P,C,E,D$ (which has diameter $PE$) lies on line $PE$ and on the perpendicular bisector of $CD$, which is the line through $O$ perpendicular to $CD$; so it is $F$. Therefore $F$ is the midpoint of $PE$, and with $O$ the midpoint of $AB$, $OF$ is a diameter of the nine-point circle of $\triangle PAB$, i.e. $OF$ equals the circumradius of $\triangle PAB$.

Since $\angle PAB=50^\circ$ and $\angle PBA=70^\circ$, $\angle APB=60^\circ$. By the law of sines $OF=\frac{AB}{2\sin60^\circ}=\frac2{\sqrt3}=\frac{2\sqrt3}3$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-10.title: Coordinates
cmimc-2024-geometry-10.body:
Put $O$ at the origin, $A=(-1,0)$, $B=(1,0)$, $C=(\cos100^\circ,\sin100^\circ)$, $D=(\cos40^\circ,\sin40^\circ)$. Computing $E$, the perpendicular from $O$ to $CD$ and the vertical line through $E$ numerically gives $OF=1.1547=\frac{2}{\sqrt3}$.

**Answer: $\frac{2\sqrt3}{3}$**

cmimc-2024-geometry-11.title: Exact volume
cmimc-2024-geometry-11.body:
This is an estimation tiebreaker (closest answer wins). Put the sphere at the origin. The octahedron is $|x|+|y|+|z|\le1$ (volume $\frac43$) and the cube is $|x|,|y|,|z|\le\frac1{\sqrt3}$. The intersection is the octahedron with its six tips beyond $|x|=\frac1{\sqrt3}$ (etc.) removed. Each tip has volume $\int_{a}^1 2(1-x)^2dx=\frac23(1-a)^3$ with $a=\frac1{\sqrt3}$, so the intersection has volume $\frac43-4(1-a)^3=\frac43\left(1-3\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)^3\right)$. Dividing by $\frac43\pi$ gives $\frac1\pi\left(1-3\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt3}\right)^3\right)\approx0.246214$.

**Answer: $\approx0.246214$**
